warmup.q: interface Source<T> { fun next(): T } and fun total(s: Source<Payment>). You have a Source<CardPayment>. What do you need for total(cards) to compile?
options: Nothing: CardPayment is a Payment, so it already compiles
Declare interface Source<out T>, because Source only hands T out
Cast: total(cards as Source<Payment>) is the normal way
warmup.why: Generic types are invariant unless you say otherwise, so the call does not compile yet. Source only produces T, so a source of card payments can safely act as a source of payments. out tells the compiler that. in is for the opposite case, consumers, which lesson 5 of this track covers.

sections.h: A producer only hands values out
sections.html:
A producer is a type whose values of T only ever come out of it. A feed of payments, a page of search results, an iterator, a Supplier. You call it, and it hands you a T. Nothing about it takes a T in.

Run the substitution test from lesson 3 of this track on a producer. Suppose some code expects a source of Payment, and you hand it a source of CardPayment. Every call it can make returns a CardPayment, and every CardPayment is a Payment. Nothing can go wrong. So it is safe to treat a Source<CardPayment> as a Source<Payment>.

The compiler can't see that by itself. Generic types are invariant unless you say otherwise. In Kotlin you say otherwise on the declaration, once, with out. Java has no such keyword, so it says it at every use with ? extends:

Java
interface Source<T> {
    T next();                                       // null when empty
}

static long totalCents(Source<? extends Payment> source) { ... }

Source<Card> cards = listSource(List.of(card1, card2));
totalCents(cards);                                  // fine: the parameter says ? extends
Source<Payment> plain = cards;                      // error: Source<Card> cannot be converted to Source<Payment>
Kotlin
interface Source<out T> {
    fun next(): T?                                  // null when empty
}

fun totalCents(source: Source<Payment>): Long { ... }

val cards: Source<CardPayment> = ListSource(listOf(card1, card2))
totalCents(cards)                                   // fine: Source is declared out
val plain: Source<Payment> = cards                  // also fine

Remove the out and Kotlin behaves like Java's plain Source<T>:

error: argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Source<CardPayment>', but 'Source<Payment>' was expected.

This property is called covariance: the subtype arrow between the element types carries over, in the same direction, to the generic type. CardPayment is a subtype of Payment, so Source<CardPayment> is a subtype of Source<Payment>. The figure shows the two arrows side by side.

Where you put out matters. Kotlin's out on the declaration is called declaration-site variance. You think about it once, when you write Source, and every user gets the flexible behaviour for free. Java's ? extends is use-site variance: every method that takes a source must remember to write it, and the ones that forget are stricter than they need to be. Lesson 6 of this track shows that Kotlin has the use-site form too, for types that can't be out everywhere.

try.title: Take out away and watch the call break
steps: Run ProducerDemo (or ProducerDemoJava) with the command below. Both print the same totals.
In ProducerDemo.kt, remove out from both interface Source<out T> and class ListSource<out T>. Predict which line fails, then run.
Put out back. In the Java twin, uncomment the wrong move. Why does Java need ? extends on totalCents while Kotlin needs nothing there?

code.title: ProducerDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.generics.l04.demo interface Payment { val id: String; val cents: Long } data class CardPayment(override val id: String, override val cents: Long, val last4: String) : Payment data class BankTransfer(override val id: String, override val cents: Long, val iban: String) : Payment /** A producer: T only comes out. `out` tells the compiler so. */ interface Source<out T> { fun next(): T? // null when there is nothing left } class ListSource<out T>(items: List<T>) : Source<T> { private val it = items.iterator() override fun next(): T? = if (it.hasNext()) it.next() else null } /** Needs a Source<Payment>. Because Source is `out`, a Source<CardPayment> fits. */ fun totalCents(source: Source<Payment>): Long { var sum = 0L while (true) { val p = source.next() ?: break sum += p.cents } return sum } fun main() { val cards: Source<CardPayment> = ListSource(listOf(CardPayment("pay_1", 1_200, "4242"), CardPayment("pay_2", 350, "0005"))) println("card total: ${totalCents(cards)}") // a Source<CardPayment> used as a Source<Payment> val anything: Source<Any> = ListSource(listOf("EUR")) // Source<String> used as Source<Any> println("first of anything: ${anything.next()}") }

alt.title: ProducerDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.generics.l04.demo; import java.util.Iterator; import java.util.List; /** * Java twin of ProducerDemo.kt. Java has no `out` on a declaration, so Source<T> stays invariant * and every method that wants "a source of some kind of Payment" says so at the use site: ? extends. */ public class ProducerDemoJava { record Card(String id, long cents) implements Payment { public String getId() { return id; } public long getCents() { return cents; } } interface Source<T> { T next(); // null when there is nothing left } static <T> Source<T> listSource(List<T> items) { Iterator<T> it = items.iterator(); return () -> it.hasNext() ? it.next() : null; } // ? extends Payment: "a Source of Payment or of some subtype". Without it, a Source<Card> would not fit. static long totalCents(Source<? extends Payment> source) { long sum = 0; for (Payment p = source.next(); p != null; p = source.next()) sum += p.getCents(); return sum; } public static void main(String[] args) { Source<Card> cards = listSource(List.of(new Card("pay_1", 1_200), new Card("pay_2", 350))); System.out.println("card total: " + totalCents(cards)); Source<? extends Object> anything = listSource(List.of("EUR")); System.out.println("first of anything: " + anything.next()); // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // Source<Payment> plain = cards; } }

try.expect: Both versions print card total: 1550 and first of anything: EUR. Without out, Kotlin fails on totalCents(cards) with Argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Source<CardPayment>', but 'Source<Payment>' was expected. The Java wrong move fails with incompatible types: Source<Card> cannot be converted to Source<Payment>. Java's Source<T> is invariant, so each method that wants flexibility writes ? extends. Kotlin wrote out once on the interface.

video.title: A producer only hands values out, so the subtype arrow keeps its direction

sections.h: Every member has a position: in, out or invariant
sections.html:
out is a promise: "values of T only come out of this type". The compiler holds you to it by checking where T appears in each public member. Every place has a position:

  • A return type is an out-position. The value flows out to the caller.
  • A parameter type is an in-position. The value flows in from the caller.
  • A var property is both at once, because it has a getter and a setter. That is an invariant position.

In a class declared out T, T may appear only in out-positions. Try to break it, and the error names the position:

Java
// Java has no `out` on the declaration, so it checks the same rule where you USE the type:
interface Producer<T> {
    T produce();
    void consume(T item);
}

Producer<? extends Object> view = strings;
Object out = view.produce();     // fine: T comes out
view.consume("USD");             // error: String cannot be converted to CAP#1
Kotlin
interface Producer<out T> {
    fun produce(): T             // fine
    val latest: T                // fine: a val only has a getter
    fun consume(item: T)         // error: ... declared as 'out' but occurs in 'in' position
    var current: T               // error: ... declared as 'out' but occurs in 'invariant' position
}

The full Kotlin message reads type parameter 'T' is declared as 'out' but occurs in 'in' position in type 'T (of interface Producer<out T>)'. Java's CAP#1 is javac's name for "the unknown subtype behind ? extends". Java can't promise any String fits it, so it refuses the call.

Three special cases come up all the time in Kotlin.

Constructor parameters are fine, as long as they are plain parameters or val properties. class Holder<out T>(val item: T, plain: T) compiles. Building the object puts a T in, but only once, when the real type is still known. A var constructor property is a var, so class Mutable<out T>(var item: T) fails with the invariant-position error.

Private members are exempt. private var hidden: T and private fun replace(t: T) are allowed, because no outside code can call them with the wrong type. protected and internal members are checked like public ones.

private set is not enough. var lastServed: T? = null; private set still fails, with occurs in 'invariant' position. The property is still a var. The fix is to split it: a private var for the class and a public val that reads it. The lab makes you do exactly that.

try.title: Find the positions the compiler rejects
steps: Open PositionsDemo.kt. For the four numbered lines, predict the position the error will name: in or invariant.
Uncomment each line on its own and run. Comment it out again before the next.
Run PositionsDemoJava and uncomment its view.consume line. Where does Java report the same rule?

code.title: PositionsDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.generics.l04.demo /** Which members may mention T in a class declared `out T`? Uncomment ONE line at a time and run. */ interface Producer<out T> { fun produce(): T // return type: out-position, fine val latest: T // val: out-position, fine // fun consume(item: T) // 1 // var current: T // 2 } class Holder<out T>(val item: T, plain: T, private var hidden: T) { // all three are fine private fun replace(t: T) { hidden = t } // private: exempt fun first(): T = item // protected fun keep(t: T) {} // 3 } // class Mutable<out T>(var item: T) // 4 fun main() { val h: Holder<Any> = Holder("EUR", "x", "y") println("Holder<String> used as Holder<Any>: ${h.first()}") }

Java cannot mark a declaration `out`, so the same rule shows up * where you USE the type: through a `? extends` reference you may call methods that return T, * and javac refuses calls that pass a T in. */ public class PositionsDemoJava { interface Producer<T> { T produce(); void consume(T item); // allowed in the declaration: Java checks the use site } public static void main(String[] args) { Producer<String> strings = new Producer<>() { String last = "EUR"; public String produce() { return last; } public void consume(String item) { last = item; } }; Producer<? extends Object> view = strings; // the Java spelling of "used as Producer<out Any>" Object out = view.produce(); // fine: out-position System.out.println("produced " + out); // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // view.consume("USD"); } }

The demo itself prints Holder<String> used as Holder<Any>: EUR. Java reports the rule at the call: String cannot be converted to CAP#1, because Java checks variance where you use a type, not where you declare it.

sections.h: List<out E> is Kotlin's answer to ? extends
sections.html:
You have used a covariant type every day: Kotlin's read-only List. Its declaration is public interface List<out E> : Collection<E>. That out is why a List<CardPayment> goes into any function that takes a List<Payment>, with no ceremony.

Java
static long sumCents(List<? extends Payment> payments) {    // the wildcard is the flexible part
    long sum = 0;
    for (Payment p : payments) sum += p.getCents();
    return sum;
}

static long sumCentsInvariant(List<Payment> payments) { ... }

List<CardPayment> cards = new ArrayList<>(List.of(card1, card2));
sumCents(cards);              // fine
sumCentsInvariant(cards);     // error: List<CardPayment> cannot be converted to List<Payment>
Kotlin
fun sumCents(payments: List<Payment>): Long = payments.sumOf { it.cents }

fun sumCentsMutable(payments: MutableList<Payment>): Long = payments.sumOf { it.cents }

val cards: MutableList<CardPayment> = mutableListOf(card1, card2)
sumCents(cards)               // fine: List is out
sumCentsMutable(cards)        // error: actual type is 'MutableList<CardPayment>', but 'MutableList<Payment>' was expected

The two snippets line up exactly. Java's List<? extends Payment> and Kotlin's List<Payment> are the same contract: "a list I will only read from, of Payment or any subtype". Java's plain List<Payment> and Kotlin's MutableList<Payment> are the strict, invariant version.

Kotlin keeps this promise when Java code calls it. When a parameter's type is declared out, Kotlin writes a ? extends into the Java signature. javap shows it (package names shortened):

public static final long sumCents(java.util.List<? extends Payment>);
public static final long sumCentsMutable(java.util.List<Payment>);

So Java callers can pass a List<CardPayment> to sumCents too. Kotlin skips the wildcard in two places: in return types, so Java callers don't have to handle wildcards, and when the type argument is a final class like String, where ? extends String would mean nothing. The lab's tests use this rule to check your out: they read the Java signature of your function and look for ? extends.

refs.title: Variant generics in Java signatures (Calling Kotlin from Java)

sections.html:
The most common wrong idea about covariance is that out means read-only, or immutable. It doesn't. out only limits which types can flow in. State can still change. This compiles and empties the shelf:

Java
List<CardPayment> cards = new ArrayList<>(List.of(card1, card2));
List<? extends Payment> view = cards;      // "read-only" for the type only

Payment taken = view.remove(0);            // fine: remove hands a value out
view.clear();                              // fine: no T involved
view.add(card3);                           // error: CardPayment cannot be converted to CAP#1
Kotlin
class Shelf<out T>(private val items: MutableList<T>) {
    fun take(): T = items.removeAt(0)      // changes state, only hands T out
    fun clear() = items.clear()            // changes state, no T at all
}

val view: MutableList<out Payment> = mutableListOf(card1, card2)
view.removeAt(0)                           // fine
view.clear()                               // fine
view.add(card3)                            // error: contains out projection which prohibits the use of 'fun add(element: E)'

Shelf holds a private MutableList<T>, which is allowed because private members are exempt. take() removes an item and still only hands a T out. clear() mentions no T at all. Both are legal in an out class. The Kotlin docs say it plainly: the only thing variance guarantees is type safety, and immutability is a different story.

So when you need a class to be covariant but it also seems to need a method that takes a T, you have three honest options:

  1. Move the method out of the class as an extension function. fun <T> Feed<T>.nextOr(fallback: T): T declares its own T, so the class's variance rules don't apply. The standard library does this: plus(element: T) and getOrElse on List are extensions.
  2. Give the method its own type parameter, such as fun <R> map(f: (T) -> R): Page<R>. Here T sits inside the parameter of a function parameter, and two in-positions cancel out. Lesson 5 of this track shows why.
  3. Split the type in two: a covariant read interface and an invariant read-write one, like List and MutableList.

There is also @UnsafeVariance, which switches the check off for one position. List.contains(element: @UnsafeVariance E) uses it, because contains only compares. It is a promise you make by hand, and lesson 10 of this track shows how to break it.

try.title: Empty a covariant shelf
steps: Run ImmutableMythDemo (or ImmutableMythDemoJava). Before it runs, predict whether take() and clear() compile in a class declared out T.
Uncomment the view.add line and run. Read which rule stops it.

code.title: ImmutableMythDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.generics.l04.demo /** `out` limits which TYPES flow in. It does not stop state from changing. */ class Shelf<out T>(private val items: MutableList<T>) { // a private MutableList<T> is fine in an out class fun take(): T = items.removeAt(0) // changes state, still only hands T out fun clear() = items.clear() // changes state, mentions no T at all val size: Int get() = items.size } fun main() { val shelf: Shelf<Payment> = Shelf(mutableListOf(CardPayment("pay_1", 1_200, "4242"), CardPayment("pay_2", 350, "0005"))) println("took ${shelf.take().id}, ${shelf.size} left") shelf.clear() println("after clear: ${shelf.size} left") // The same is true of a use-site out projection: no add, but clear and removeAt still work. val view: MutableList<out Payment> = mutableListOf(CardPayment("pay_3", 99, "1111")) view.removeAt(0) println("view after removeAt: ${view.size} left") // view.add(CardPayment("pay_4", 10, "2222")) // uncomment: which rule stops this? }

alt.title: ImmutableMythDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.generics.l04.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** Java twin of ImmutableMythDemo.kt. A ? extends view stops adds, not changes. */ public class ImmutableMythDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { List<CardPayment> cards = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new CardPayment("pay_1", 1_200, "4242"), new CardPayment("pay_2", 350, "0005"))); List<? extends Payment> view = cards; // read-only for the TYPE, not for the state Payment taken = view.remove(0); // compiles: remove hands a value out System.out.println("took " + taken.getId() + ", " + view.size() + " left"); view.clear(); // compiles: no T involved System.out.println("after clear: " + view.size() + " left, and cards has " + cards.size()); // view.add(new CardPayment("pay_4", 10, "2222")); // uncomment: which rule stops this? } }

try.expect: It prints took pay_1, 1 left, after clear: 0 left and, in Kotlin, view after removeAt: 0 left. Variance never stopped the state from changing. The add fails with Receiver type 'MutableList<out Payment>' contains out projection which prohibits the use of 'fun add(element: E): Boolean'. in Kotlin and CardPayment cannot be converted to CAP#1 in Java: only the in-position is blocked.

analogy: A covariant type is a vending machine. A machine that dispenses only cola can stand in for "a drinks machine": everyone who asks it for a drink gets a drink. What you must not do is let customers load their own cans into it. If the cola machine took returns, someone could load lemonade into it through the "drinks machine" label, and the next person who wanted cola would get lemonade. out is the rule that the machine has no loading slot for customers. The analogy breaks at one point: a real vending machine can still be emptied, restocked by staff or switched off. out says nothing about any of that. It only controls which type of can goes in through the public slot.
world: Most read-side types in a payment service are producers: a page of results from the ledger API, a Feed of settlement records, a query result, a read-only snapshot of balances. Declare them out (or keep them as Kotlin Lists) and a Page<CardPayment> drops straight into reporting code that expects a Page<Payment>. In a Quarkus REST client written in Java you will see the same contract as List<? extends PaymentDto> in parameters. When you write a Kotlin library that Java services call, Kotlin adds those wildcards to parameters for you, so Java callers get the same flexibility.
mistake: The common mistake is to read out as "immutable" and then trust a covariant type to protect shared state. A MutableList<out Payment> still has clear() and removeAt(), and a class Shelf<out T> can wrap a private mutable list. People make this mistake because the C# and Kotlin keywords sound like access rules. They are type rules. The fix is to keep two questions apart: "can a subtype stand in for the supertype here?" (variance) and "can anyone change this?" (expose a read-only interface, or copy). The other mistake is the reverse: giving up on out because one method takes a T. Move that method to an extension function, or split the type into a read interface and a write interface.

compare.title: A producer, declared once in Kotlin, spelled at each use in Java

java.title: Feeds.java
java.html: import java.util.List; interface Payment { long cents(); } record CardPayment(long cents) implements Payment {} // Java can't say "T only comes out" on the declaration interface Source<T> { T next(); } class Feeds { // every method that should accept subtypes must remember ? extends static long total(Source<? extends Payment> source, int n) { long sum = 0; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) sum += source.next().cents(); return sum; } static long sum(List<? extends Payment> payments) { return payments.stream().mapToLong(Payment::cents).sum(); } // forget it once and the method is stricter than it needs to be static long strict(Source<Payment> source) { return source.next().cents(); } }

kotlin.title: Feeds.kt
kotlin.html: interface Payment { val cents: Long } data class CardPayment(override val cents: Long) : Payment // say it once, on the declaration interface Source<out T> { fun next(): T } // plain types in every signature: Source and List are both covariant fun total(source: Source<Payment>, n: Int): Long { var sum = 0L repeat(n) { sum += source.next().cents } return sum } fun sum(payments: List<Payment>): Long = payments.sumOf { it.cents } // the compiler enforces the promise inside Source: // fun push(t: T) would fail with "declared as 'out' but occurs in 'in' position"

compare.note: The safety rule is the same in both languages: through a covariant view you may take values out but not put them in. The difference is who carries the burden. In Java the type stays invariant and every method signature has to say ? extends, so the flexibility depends on each author remembering. In Kotlin the author of Source says out once, the compiler checks every member of Source against it, and every signature that mentions Source<Payment> is automatically flexible. When Java calls that Kotlin code, Kotlin writes the ? extends into the parameter types for it.

worked.title: Make a settlement Feed covariant without losing a feature

steps.say: A settlement job reads payments from a Feed. Reporting code wants a Feed<Payment>, but the job has a Feed<CardPayment>. The feed only hands items out, so it should be covariant. Here it is before the change.
steps.code: class Feed<T>(items: List<T>) { private val queue = ArrayDeque(items) var lastServed: T? = null private set fun next(): T { val item = queue.removeFirst(); lastServed = item; return item } fun nextOr(fallback: T): T = if (queue.isEmpty()) fallback else next() }

alt.html: class Feed<T> { private final ArrayDeque<T> queue; private T lastServed; Feed(List<T> items) { queue = new ArrayDeque<>(items); } T next() { T item = queue.removeFirst(); lastServed = item; return item; } T nextOr(T fallback) { return queue.isEmpty() ? fallback : next(); } T lastServed() { return lastServed; } }

steps.say: 1. Add out and read the errors. The compiler names two members. nextOr takes a T (in-position). lastServed is a var, so its type is in an invariant position, even with a private setter. In Java there is nothing to add to the class; each caller writes Feed<? extends Payment> instead.
steps.code: class Feed<out T>(items: List<T>) { // error: ... declared as 'out' but occurs in 'invariant' position in type 'T?' var lastServed: T? = null private set // error: ... declared as 'out' but occurs in 'in' position in type 'T' fun nextOr(fallback: T): T = ... }

alt.html: // Java checks at the use site instead: static List<Payment> drainAll(Feed<? extends Payment> feed) { ... } Feed<? extends Payment> view = cardFeed; Payment p = view.next(); // fine view.nextOr(new BankTransfer(...)); // error: cannot be converted to CAP#1

steps.say: 1. Fix the property by splitting it: a private var (exempt) and a public val (an out-position). Callers still read lastServed, and nobody outside could set it before either.
steps.code: private var last: T? = null val lastServed: T? get() = last

alt.html: private T last; T lastServed() { return last; } // Java: a getter with no setter

steps.say: 1. Fix nextOr by moving it out of the class as an extension. The extension declares its own T, so the class's out doesn't constrain it. Self-check: why is this safe? (At the call feed.nextOr(x), the compiler picks a T that fits both the feed and x. For a Feed<CardPayment> and a BankTransfer fallback, that T is Payment, and the result is typed Payment.)
steps.code: fun <T> Feed<T>.nextOr(fallback: T): T = if (hasNext()) next() else fallback val cardFeed: Feed<CardPayment> = Feed(cards) val p: Payment = cardFeed.nextOr(BankTransfer("pay_9", 0, "DE89...")) // T = Payment

alt.html: // Java: a static helper with its own <T> does the same job static <T> T nextOr(Feed<? extends T> feed, T fallback) { return feed.hasNext() ? feed.next() : fallback; } Payment p = nextOr(cardFeed, new BankTransfer("pay_9", 0, "DE89..."));

lab.title: Make Feed and Page covariant
steps: Run the tests. Eight of nine fail. Read the two variance failures: expected "Feed<? extends Payment>" but was "Feed<Payment>". The test reads the Java signature of drainAll, which only gets a wildcard when Feed is declared out.
In Feed.kt, add out to Feed's type parameter. Run the tests and read the compile error about lastServed.
Fix lastServed without making it settable from outside: split it into a private var and a public val with a getter.
In Page.kt, add out to Page. Predict whether map still compiles before you run. Then write map and firstOnPage.
Run the tests until all nine pass.
hints: private var last: T? = null plus val lastServed: T? get() = last keeps the read for callers and the write for the class.
ArrayDeque.removeFirst() throws NoSuchElementException on an empty deque, which is what next() should do.
map compiles under out: in f: (T) -> R, T is the parameter of a parameter, which counts as an out-position. Page(items.map(f), nextCursor) is the whole body.

drill.title: Write a producer from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a covariant Source interface with one method next(), a ListSource class that implements it over a List, and a function totalCents that accepts a source of card payments as a source of payments. Write it in Kotlin with out, then in Java with ? extends. Then add a push(t: T) member to the Kotlin interface and write down the error you expect.

answer.html: interface Source<out T> { fun next(): T? } class ListSource<out T>(items: List<T>) : Source<T> { private val it = items.iterator() override fun next(): T? = if (it.hasNext()) it.next() else null } fun totalCents(source: Source<Payment>): Long { var sum = 0L while (true) sum += (source.next() ?: break).cents return sum } // fun push(t: T) inside Source: // error: type parameter 'T' is declared as 'out' but occurs in 'in' position

alt.title: Source.java
alt.html: interface Source<T> { T next(); // null when empty } static <T> Source<T> listSource(List<T> items) { Iterator<T> it = items.iterator(); return () -> it.hasNext() ? it.next() : null; } // the flexibility lives in the parameter, not in Source static long totalCents(Source<? extends Payment> source) { long sum = 0; for (Payment p = source.next(); p != null; p = source.next()) sum += p.cents(); return sum; }

recap: A producer only hands values of T out. A producer of a subtype can safely stand in for a producer of the supertype: that is covariance.
Kotlin declares it once with out T (declaration-site). Java writes ? extends T at every use (use-site).
In an out class, T may appear in return types and vals, not in parameters or vars. Constructor vals and private members are fine; private set is not enough.
Kotlin's read-only List<out E> is why List<CardPayment> fits a List<Payment> parameter. Java needs List<? extends Payment> for the same thing.
Kotlin writes ? extends into Java parameter signatures for out types, except for final type arguments and return types.
out controls which types flow in, not whether state changes. A covariant type can still be cleared.

explain.prompt: In your own words, explain to a teammate why Kotlin lets a Page<CardPayment> be passed where a Page<Payment> is expected once Page is declared out T, and what the compiler gives up in return.
explain.answer: Page only hands items out: you read items and map them, and nothing in its public API takes a T in. If I give you a page of card payments where you expected a page of payments, every item you read really is a payment, so nothing can go wrong. out T is my promise that this is true, and in return the compiler lets the subtype arrow carry over from CardPayment to Page<CardPayment>. To keep the promise honest, the compiler rejects any public member where T would flow in, like a parameter of type T or a var. In Java the same idea is written at each use as Page<? extends Payment>.

deeper.html:
The rule "parameters are in-positions" has a twist when the parameter is itself a function. In fun <R> map(f: (T) -> R), T is the input of f. The page calls f and passes it a T, so the value flows out of the page into the caller's lambda. Two in-positions cancel out. That is why map is legal in Page<out T>, while fun replay(): (T) -> Unit (a function returned to the caller, which the caller will feed a T) is not. Lesson 5 of this track turns this into a sign rule.

Kotlin is strict about inferred types too. In class E<in T> { private fun produce(): T? = null; fun use() = produce() }, the private produce is fine, but the public use() has the inferred return type T? and fails. Give public members of variant classes explicit types.

Private members get one more rule, called private-to-this. Inside class C<out T>(private var t: T), the method fun copyFrom(o: C<@UnsafeVariance T>) { t = o.t } fails with cannot access 'var t: T': it is private/*private to this*/. A private member is only exempt when you reach it through this, because another instance o might really be a C<Subtype> seen as a C<T>.

Finally, Kotlin leaves the wildcard out of Java signatures when the type argument is final. fun f(x: List<String>) is f(List<String>) in Java, because nothing can extend String. Use @JvmWildcard to force one, or @JvmSuppressWildcards to drop them.
